prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B018 as a single-part prize for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, with HgTe named in the citation. After the full first-round exchange I hold it with more confidence on the science, because nobody has questioned the physics or the maturity. The Z2 classification replaced the idea that insulators are all alike with a distinction that comes from band topology and time-reversal symmetry. It predicted a concrete observable, helical edge conduction. Molenkamp's group measured that in 2007, and about two decades of transport, ARPES and STM work in several material families have confirmed it. Band-structure calculations reproduce the edge and surface spectra quantitatively, which is the kind of theory-to-measurement agreement I trust most. The chair asks whether this leaves room after the 2016 prize. I think it does. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were recognised for topological ideas in phase transitions and in quantum Hall-type states that break time-reversal symmetry, or in 2D classical systems. The 2005 Kane-Mele paper and the HgTe experiment concern a symmetry-protected insulator with no external magnetic field. It was proposed on the basis of spin-orbit coupling in real band structures and was then found in a real material. That is a separate experimental discovery, not a refinement. The citation should say so by naming the Z2 class, the quantum spin Hall state and HgTe, and by claiming nothing about 3D materials or the anomalous Hall effect.
statement.case_against: The attribution gap is the real weakness and I do not want to hide it. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang 2006 proposal told Molenkamp which quantum-well structure and which thickness to grow. Zhang died in 2018, and Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan carry the 3D case, so a three-name prize cannot reflect the full history. The citation must therefore be narrow, and the committee record should say openly that BHZ and the 3D work are context and not part of the citation. A second weakness is that edge quantisation in HgTe is only close to ideal in short channels, and practical impact is modest. A third is that I am a condensed-matter theorist and members from other fields may be deferring to me and to Mehlig on a case that suits our field. I cannot check the primary papers in this exercise, so my recollection of the decisive step for the HgTe experiment is from memory.

responses.point: Kroll holds B041 first and says the Katori-Ye credit is clean, while calling the B018 attribution gap (BHZ and the 3D work) more troubling than the overlap with earlier clock prizes, and says he would move B018 to a close second if the allocation were resolved convincingly.
responses.response: Your argument for B041 is the best-attributed case on the list and I keep it as my first alternative. I would like to answer the attribution point directly. The Nobel statutes cap us at three names, so a prize gets honoured on the decisive steps. For B018 those are the Z2 class and the quantum spin Hall prediction (Kane and Mele) and the first observation (Molenkamp). BHZ determined the material platform but did not introduce the topological class, and the 3D work is a different, later discovery that a narrow citation need not cover. That is a smaller gap than a missing proposer. I also still think B041 carries a novelty problem. The 2005 and 2012 prizes already honoured the comb and the control of single-ion clocks, and the lattice clock's fundamental-physics results so far are constraints. If the committee can show me that the lattice concept is the discovery and not the performance record, I will reconsider, but I do not yet see that in the exchange.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B032 to B018 and raises the worry that topological band theory belongs to the lineage already rewarded in 2016, while also saying the committee should read the Molenkamp paper alongside BHZ to decide whether the experimental credit is Molenkamp's alone.
responses.response: I welcome your move and your questions, and I take the 2016 worry seriously. My answer is that the 2016 prize recognised topological invariants in phase transitions and in quantum Hall-type matter. B018 is a new state, a time-reversal-invariant topological insulator that exists in an ordinary non-magnetic semiconductor and has been observed in several materials, so a prize here complements the earlier one. On the priority question, we should compare the two papers. As I recall, BHZ proposed the HgTe/CdTe well and the critical thickness at which the band inversion occurs. Molenkamp's group then built the structures and measured the conductance plateau and its non-local behaviour. The experiment is therefore genuinely theirs even though the proposal came from someone else. I would be comfortable with a note in the committee record, provided the citation says 'first experimental observation' and not 'discovery of the effect'.

responses.point: The chair moved from IceCube to B018, asks whether a narrow citation is defensible without BHZ, and asks whether a precision-measurement pairing with a second part could be configured under the three-person limit.
responses.response: Thank you for the direct question, which I put to myself too. Yes, I think the narrow citation is defensible without BHZ, for the reasons I give above, but I would say plainly that it is a choice and that it leaves a visible gap. On pairing, I do not favour a two-part prize at this point. A second part such as B041 would need two names, and the combined total of five people would break the three-person limit across the configuration. Dropping Molenkamp or Mele to make room would be much more arbitrary than the BHZ omission, because it would break the theory-experiment link that makes B018 persuasive. A single well-argued part seems to me stronger than two unequal ones.

responses.point: Lindroth holds B041 first, with B018 as her first alternative, and defers to the condensed-matter members on how central the quantum spin Hall effect is.
responses.response: Thank you for the deference, but I would not want the committee to rely on it without checking. The condensed-matter members are the ones most likely to overrate this field, and it is useful that Danielsson, Johansson and the chair have independently come to B018 from other fields. For the clocks, your account of reproducibility across Sr, Yb and Hg is persuasive, and I do not dispute that B041 is mature. What I remain unsure of is whether it is a new discovery or an improved instrument. If you could say what unexpected physics the lattice clock revealed, as opposed to confirming general relativity or improving a bound, that would be the best evidence for your side.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 class, with BHZ, Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan acknowledged as context and not credited.
Whether my recollection of the BHZ and Molenkamp chronology, which I cannot check against the primary papers here, would survive review by an external expert.
Whether B041 is stronger than I judge, since atomic physics lies outside my core expertise and the question of Katori's concept versus Ye's performance is unresolved.
Whether the support for B018 is inflated by condensed-matter members' familiarity and not by its standing against atomic-physics and astrophysics cases.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. I have no stated personal, supervisory or institutional connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye, MacDonald or Jarillo-Herrero. My Uppsala and Wallenberg funding and my theory work on magnetism and spectra are general background and not a tie to any credited name. I note that Johansson, Kroll, Mehlig and Olsson have disclosed Chalmers and Gothenburg links; none of these touches B018.
